choices.correct_explanation:
• Herd immunity (community immunity) refers to the indirect protection of unvaccinated individuals when a large portion of the population is immune to a communicable disease, thereby reducing transmission.
  • However, tetanus is not a communicable disease—it is caused by Clostridium tetani spores found in soil, dust, or animal feces, which enter the body through wounds or cuts.
  • Since tetanus does not spread from person to person, herd immunity has no role in its prevention.
  • Protection against tetanus depends solely on individual immunization with the TT (Tetanus Toxoid) vaccine or Td/Tdap.

choices.title: Acute pain
choices.correct_explanation:
·         Acute pain is a sudden, intense nociceptive stimulus that instantly activates the sympathetic nervous system. Adrenaline and noradrenaline flood the bloodstream within seconds, causing mydriasis (pupil dilation to improve vision), vasoconstriction (elevated blood pressure), and sinus tachycardia (heart rate >100 bpm). This exact triad is taught as the classic “acute pain response” in every nursing and medical textbook.         

Explanation for the incorrect options: 

·         Chronic pain lasts >3 months; the sympathetic system is exhausted, so pupils, BP, and HR return to baseline. Neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia) is a nerve misfire with no sympathetic storm pupils stay normal. Visceral pain (appendicitis, cholecystitis) may raise BP slightly, but pupils remain normal unless the pain becomes acute and perforates.

choices.title: Alert line
choices.correct_explanation:
• In partograph (cervicography crossing), two important lines are drawn on the graph that records cervical dilatation vs. time during labor:

Alert Line

  • Represents the expected rate of cervical dilatation in a woman progressing normally in labor (approximately 1 cm/hour in active phase).
  • Drawn from 4 cm cervical dilatation to full dilatation (10 cm).
  • If the plotting of cervical dilatation remains to the left of the alert line, labor is progressing normally.
  • If the plotting crosses the alert line, it means labor is slower than expected, and the woman should be transferred to a higher centre or closely monitored.

Action Line

  • Drawn parallel and 4 hours to the right of the alert line.
  • If the plotting of cervical dilatation crosses the action line, it indicates abnormal or prolonged labor.
  • Immediate evaluation and intervention (e.g., augmentation or cesarean section) are required.

Key nursing discharge instructions for home care:

·         Inspect the jejunostomy site daily for:

o   Redness, swelling, or purulent discharge (signs of infection)

o   Leakage of intestinal contents (risk of skin irritation and dehydration)

o   Integrity and patency of the tube

·         Maintain skin integrity:

o   Clean gently with mild soap and water or normal saline—avoid alcohol or hydrogen peroxide.

o   Keep the area dry; apply protective barrier cream if prescribed.

·         Ensure adequate hydration and nutrition:

o   Monitor for increased stoma output, which can lead to fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

o   Use prescribed jejunostomy feeds (not oral or high-calorie formulas unless advised).

  • Prevent tube dislodgement or blockage by securing it properly and flushing as directed.

·         Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of skin/mucosa) appears only when deoxygenated hemoglobin exceeds 5 g/dL — indicating significant hypoxemia. It reflects prolonged inadequate oxygenation and impending respiratory failure.

Physiological Explanation

choices.correct_explanation:
·         Initial serum bilirubin = 15 mg/dL

·         Expected rate of reduction with effective phototherapy = 1–2 mg/dL every 4–6 hours

·         Duration of therapy = 12 hours

Step 1: Determine the number of 4–6 hour intervals in 12 hours

12 hours ÷ 4–6 hours per interval = 2 intervals (approximately)

 Step 2: Calculate total reduction over 12 hours 

·         Minimum reduction: 1 mg/dL× 2 = 2 mg/dL  

·         Maximum reduction: 2 mg/dL 2 = 4 mg/dL

So, total expected reduction = 2–4 mg/dL

Step 3: Subtract from initial bilirubin

                        15 mg/dL−(2–4 mg/dL) = 11–13 mg/dL

However, since phototherapy can be more effective (especially with intensive blue-light units), many guidelines cite a net expected fall of 3–6 mg/dL in 12–24 hours, giving a range of ~9–12 mg/dL after 12 hours.

Clinical note:   

·         Phototherapy efficacy depends on factors like lamp intensity, distance, exposed skin area, and hydration.

·         If bilirubin does not decline as expected, evaluate for ineffective phototherapy or pathologic causes (e.g., hemolysis).

Features suggestive of pathological jaundice:     

Rh incompatibility between maternal and fetal red blood cells leads to pathological jaundice.

·         Jaundice that appears in the first 24-36 hours of birth 

·         Persistent jaundice after 10-14 days of birth

·         A rise in serum bilirubin faster than 5 mg/dL / 24 hr  

·         Total serum bilirubin levels above the expected normal range; jaundice seen in the mid-abdominal region (= 15 mg/dL) and soles (= 20 mg/dL)

·         Serum bilirubin > 12 mg/dL in a full-term infant (especially if there are no risk factors)

·         Serum bilirubin > 10-14 mg/dL in a preterm infant

·         Direct bilirubin > 2 mg/dL at any time

·         Total serum bilirubin concentration not responding to phototherapy

·         Total serum bilirubin rising rapidly (i.e., crossing percentiles) in an infant receiving phototherapy

choices.title: Use a dry oxygen delivery system
Provide intermittent humidification with a heated humidifier
choices.correct_explanation:
When a child receives high-flow oxygen therapy (≥4 L/min or FiO₂ >40%), the delivered gas tends to be dry and non-humidified, which can cause:

·         Drying of airway mucosa

·         Thickening of secretions

·         Airway inflammation

·         Mucosal injury and epistaxis

Hence, humidification is essential to maintain mucociliary function and prevent airway damage.

Best practice for humidification in pediatric high-flow oxygen therapy: Use a heated humidifier (preferably active, heated type) — maintains optimal temperature (31–37°C) and relative humidity (~100%). Because:

·         Heated humidification ensures the delivered gas mimics physiological humidity of inspired air.

·         Prevents airway drying, mucus plugging, and atelectasis.

·         Recommended in High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) or high-flow oxygen systems (>4 L/min).

 

Other options:      

·         Option-a: Use a dry oxygen delivery system: Leads to airway mucosal dryness, irritation, and crusting — not recommended. 

·         Option-c: Administer saline nebulization every hour: Nebulization offers temporary humidification and does not substitute for continuous humidified flow.

·         Option-d: Use a cold mist humidifier continuously: Cold humidifiers provide inadequate humidity and may cause airway cooling, leading to bronchospasm in children.

Clinical Key:

·         Heated humidification is a standard component of modern HFNC systems.

Recommended for neonates, infants, and children requiring high FiO₂ or high flow rates.

Asthalin (salbutamol/albuterol) is a short-acting β₂-adrenergic agonist (SABA) used for bronchodilation in asthma.
In pediatric patients, correct inhalation technique is crucial to ensure the drug reaches the lower airways and produces the desired effect.

Most Important Nursing Instruction: Use a spacer device (with or without a face mask, depending on age).

·         Improves drug deposition in the lungs (up to 20–25% vs. 10% with MDI alone).

·         Reduces oropharyngeal deposition → fewer local side effects (e.g., throat irritation, tremor, tachycardia).

·         Simplifies coordination between actuation and inhalation — especially helpful for children <6 years.

·         Ensures consistent and effective dose delivery.

Steps for using MDI with spacer:

·         Shake the inhaler well.

·         Insert inhaler into the spacer.

·         Place the mouthpiece (or mask) properly.

·         Press once to release a puff.

·         Have the child take 5–6 slow deep breaths.

·         Wait 1 minute between puffs.

·         Rinse the mouth after use (to prevent throat irritation).

 

Other options:

·         Option-a: Administer only during acute asthma attacks: The doctor prescribed scheduled doses (every 6 hours), not “as needed.” Inhaled corticosteroids are usually preventive; SABAs can also be used regularly short-term.

·         Option-c: Increase to 4 puffs if symptoms worsen: Dose adjustment must be physician-directed; overuse can cause tachycardia, tremors, hypokalemia.

·         The neural tube defect in myelomeningocele often involves Arnold–Chiari II malformation, which causes obstruction of CSF flow at the level of the fourth ventricle.

·         This leads to non-communicating hydrocephalus, increasing intracranial pressure.

·         Because the cranial sutures are not yet fused in a neonate, the fontanelle bulges outward in response to elevated intracranial pressure.

choices.correct_explanation:
A meningocele is a type of spina bifida cystica in which only the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protrude through a vertebral defect, forming a sac-like cyst.
The spinal cord and nerve roots remain intact and in their normal position, unlike in myelomeningocele.

Because the neural tissue is not involved and there is no communication with the spinal cord, the CSF within the sac is normal — that is, clear and sterile, with normal cell count, glucose, and protein levels, provided there is no infection or bleeding.

Meningocele

·         Meningocele is the herniation of the meninges only through a bony cleft, most commonly in the lumbosacral region. Meningocele is usually not associated with any neural deficits.

·         Etiology: Failure of fusion of posterior neural arch

·         Clinical Features   

o   Most common in lumbosacral area.

o   A fluctuant midline mass is present overlying the spine. The mass is filled with CSF and can be transilluminated. Neurologic deficits are usually not present or are only very mild.

o   Usually no disability, low incidence of associated anomalies, and hydrocephalus.

·         Diagnosis   

o   Must determine extent of neural involvement with MRI

o   CT scan of head for possible hydrocephalus

·         Treatment: Surgical excision and tissue repair

·         Prognosis: Good prognosis with surgical treatment

choices.title: Insulin therapy
choices.correct_explanation:
Type 1 diabetes formerly referred to as insulin-dependent diabetes or juvenile diabetes. Insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process. The beta cells produce little or no insulin. People with type 1 diabetes, therefore, require an exogenous form of insulin (injections or inhaled form) in addition to diet and exercise to control blood glucose levels.

Pathophysiology of Type 1 diabetes

·         Genetic, immunologic, and possibly environmental factors contribute to beta cell destruction in the pancreas.

·         Results in decreased insulin production, unchecked glucose production by the liver, which in turn results in a fasting hyperglycemia.

·         Glucose derived from food cannot be utilized for energy and metabolic processes without insulin, causing it to remain in the bloodstream and contribute to postprandial (after meals) hyperglycemia.

·         Increased levels of sugar in the blood cause fluids to be pulled from the intracellular and interstitial spaces into the bloodstream or vascular space (osmosis).

·         Once this extra fluid circulating in the bloodstream reaches the kidneys, diuresis occurs as the kidneys try to maintain normal fluid volume; hence the term “osmotic diuresis.” The urine takes with it some of the excess sugar (glucosuria) as well as electrolytes. This can result in profound dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

·         Insulin normally inhibits glycogenolysis (breakdown of stored glucose) and gluconeogensis (production of new glucose from amino acids). With defective insulin production or action, both occur in an unrestrained fashion and further contribute to hyperglycemia.

  • Since the body is unable to utilize carbohydrates or sugar for energy, it resorts to breaking down fats, proteins, and body fat for energy; the by-product of which is ketones. This accounts for the ketoacidosis associated most commonly with type 1 diabetes.

The ductus venosus is a vital vascular shunt in fetal circulation that ensures the most oxygen-rich blood from the placenta reaches the fetal heart and brain efficiently.    

Fetal Circulation  

·         Oxygenation occurs in the placenta, not in the fetal lungs.

·         Oxygenated blood passes from placenta à umbilical veinà fetus:

  • 50% of umbilical venous blood bypasses liver à ductus venosus à IVC à right atrium à across foramen ovale à left atrium à left ventricle à ascending aorta
  • Other 50% of umbilical venous blood à portal vein à hepatic circulation à hepatic veins à IVC
  • Blood from superior vena cava (SVC) à right atrium àright ventricle à pulmonary artery à ductus arteriosus à descending aorta à lower body à umbilical arteries à placenta
  • Small amount of blood travels to pulmonary circulation

Figure: Concepts of fetal circulation    

·         Concept - 1: Oxygenated blood from placenta to the fetus via the umbilical vein.

·         Concept - 2: Most of the umbilical venous blood shunts via the ductus venosus to the inferior vena cava and gets mixed with deoxygenated blood from the lower part of the body and liver.

·         Concept - 3: One third of blood from the inferior venacava is directly pumped to the left atrium across the foramen ovale; then to the left ventricle; and ejected from there into the ascending aorta, where it supplies the upper body and the brain.   

·         Concept - 4: A major portion of blood enters the right ventricle, mixes with blood from the superior vena cava, and ejects into the pulmonary trunk.

  • Concept - 5: Ductus arteriosus bypasses the lungs, and hence, a major portion pumps into the descending aorta to perfuse the lower part of the body and the umbilical arteries carry blood to the placenta for oxygenation.

A delusion of persecution refers to a false, fixed belief that one is being harmed, conspired against, or plotted against by others. This is one of the most common types of delusions seen in schizophrenia and paranoid disorders.

Types of delusions:   

Delusion of control

False belief that a person's will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Delusion of grandeur or Megalomania

Exaggerated conception of one's importance, power, or identity.

 

Delusion of infidelity or morbid jealousy or Othello syndrome

False belief that one's lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy. 

Delusion of love or erotomania

False belief that another person is in love with him/her. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

Delusion of misidentification

·         Capgras syndrome: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an exact double i.e. an impostor.

·         Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

Nihilistic delusion

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc, it is called Cotard syndrome.

Delusion of infestation

False belief that one is infested with small but visible organisms. As a monosymptomatic delusional disorder, this is called Ekbom syndrome.

Delusion of persecution

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes they are financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about him (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

Delusion of self-accusation

False feeling of remorse and guilt. Seen in depression with psychotic features.

It is generally used for acute illnesses. It provides insight into the effectiveness of health services and programs. Incidence can be determined from cohort studies and longitudinal studies.

The incidence rate of spells of sickness = (Number of spells of sickness starting in the specified period/Mean number of people exposed to that risk in the specified time) × 1000.

Special types of incidence rates:  

1)      Attack rate: It is used when there is a risk for a limited period of time.

2)      Secondary attack rate: It is the number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of incubation period following exposure to a primary case.

 

Relationship between Incidence and Prevalence:

·         Prevalence depends upon incidence and duration.

·         Prevalence = Incidence x Mean Duration

·         Longer the duration of the disease, the greater the prevalence.

·         Few examples:

o   In acute diseases, because of rapid recovery/death prevalence will be relatively lower than incidence. This is because, in some diseases (eg. food poisoning), the disease is so short-lived, there are no "old cases".

o   In chronic diseases like TB, prevalence will be higher than incidence.

o   If a new treatment for a disease is effective, incidence does not change but prevalence decreases as the duration of disease decreases.

If the treatment only prevents death but doesn't cure the disease, it may cause a paradoxical increase in prevalence.

In COPD, respiratory acidosis occurs due to alveolar hypoventilation and CO₂ retention.

The first-line intervention is non-invasive ventilation (NIV)—most commonly BiPAP—because it:

·         Improves CO₂ removal

·         Decreases work of breathing

·         Corrects pH

·         Reduces the need for intubation

Management of COPD

·         Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) should be the first mode of ventilation used in COPD patients with acute respiratory failure provided there are no absolute contraindications. This approach improves gas exchange, reduces work of breathing and the need for intubation, decreases hospitalization duration and enhances overall survival outcomes.

·         Invasive positive pressure ventilation is only considered after failure of NIPPV, resulting in severe respiratory distress, life threatening hypoxemia, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest or hemodynamic instability.

·         Apart from NIPPV, short-acting inhaled beta 2 agonists (albuterol, salbutamol) with or without short-acting anticholinergics (ipratropium, tiotropium) are recommended as the initial bronchodilators. Maintenance therapy with long-acting beta 2 agonists (formoterol) must be started as soon as possible.

·         Systemic corticosteroids are useful in the treatment of acute exacerbations of COPD as they reduce airway inflammation and improve lung function over time. However, the effects are not immediate. NIPPV on the other hand provides immediate relief to the patient and reduces the work of breathing. Therefore, it would not be the best choice in this case.

·         Antibiotics can also be considered, as they reduce duration of hospitalisation. Treatment is given for 5 days.

·         Permissive hypercapnia refers to a ventilation strategy where tidal volume is reduced in order to avoid hyperinflation-associated lung trauma. It is not preferred at the initial presentation. It is only permitted once invasive PPV is started following NIPPV failure.

·         The aPTT is a laboratory test that characterizes blood coagulation and it is used to monitor treatment effects of patients receiving heparin.  Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) normal range 25 to 35 seconds, the therapeutic range for dosing heparin would be 1.5 to 2.5 times the normal aPTT. So the therapeutic value for aPTT is 46-70 seconds. The nurse would evaluate the aPTT for a therapeutic value and make adjustments in the rate of infusion of the heparin as needed.

·         An aPTT of 85 seconds is above the therapeutic range, indicating excess anticoagulation and increased risk of bleeding. The Appropriate action is Hold the next dose of heparin and notify the physician for dose adjustment.

Nursing Intervention Alert

·         Always check the aPTT prior to administering heparin.

·         Always check the PT and INR prior to administering Coumadin. In general, the goal is to maintain a prothrombin time (PT) of 1.5–2 times the control or reference value and maintain the international normalized ratio (INR) at a value of 2–3. The PT control value is generally 11–15 seconds.

Must knowing facts for a Nursing officer

 

                                                                    Unfractionated heparin

·         Advantages: rapidly reversible by protamine

·         Measure aPTT 6 h after the bolus

·         Before administration check coagulation tests, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet counts.

·         In general, the goal is to keep the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) at 1.5–2.5 times its normal value of 24–33 seconds.

·         Safely administer heparin via ordered route, i.e., subcutaneous injection, continuous intravenous infusion, or intermittent intravenous infusion.

·         No intramuscular injections

·         No aspirin containing products

·         Use soft toothbrush and electric razor

·         Disadvantages: Must monitor aPTT or heparin levels with adjustment of dose to reach therapeutic level (~2x normal value);

·         Repeat q24h once therapeutic

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) uncommon (3%), but serious complication; monitor platelet counts for development of HIT.

Shockable cardiac rhythm means it is VF/pulseless VT. The management of ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (shockable rhythms) is the same.  Chest compressions should be resumed immediately following shock delivery.

Pulse check and reanalysis of the cardiac rhythm is performed only after 2 minutes of chest compression and rescue breaths. This is because the heart is temporarily stunned by a defibrillator shock and so chest compressions would benefit the patient by providing coronary blood flow during this period.

For a patient with a shockable rhythm (Ventricular Fibrillation or Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia): Immediate priority is early defibrillation. Adrenaline (epinephrine) is not given immediately. It is administered after the 3rd defibrillation shock

Sequence in Shockable Rhythm:

  • 1st Shock: Delivered immediately; followed by 2 minutes of CPR.
  • 2nd Shock: Delivered if the rhythm remains shockable; followed by 2 minutes of CPR.
  • 3rd Shock: Delivered if the rhythm remains shockable. Administer Adrenaline 1mg immediately after this shock during the subsequent 2 minutes of CPR.
  • Repeat adrenaline every 3–5 minutes thereafter

 

Point to remember 

·         Epinephrine and amiodarone are the two main drugs approved by the AHA for the resuscitation of a cardiac arrest patient.

·         The first dose of epinephrine 1 mg IV is administered after the 2nd defibrillator shock is delivered and it is continued every 3-5 minutes.

·         If this is not effective, 300 mg IV bolus dose of amiodarone can be given and another dose of 150 mg given if necessary
